attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The causal reading is faithful: a liquidity crisis means VC cannot sustain AI 'forever'. The asserted premise (can't raise money, investments aren't selling) is part of the claim. 'Forever' gives no deadline.

contract.note: Reading the claim as severe constraints, not zero fundraising, is fair and ordinary. Using 2025 US data for the premise is reasonable but does not cover global VC. The result depends on the reader's view of what 'sustain' and 'forever' mean.

evidence.note: NVCA 2025 data supports the liquidity premise: exits are insufficient, LP distributions are reduced and first-time fund formation collapsed. It does not show a binding limit on AI financing.

The same release shows $67B of VC fundraising and record-level deal value, 65% of it AI. This undercuts the literal wording but does not show the constraint is non-binding long term. Much of the money came from nontraditional investors.

reviews.rationale: The packet backs the liquidity-constraint premise in ordinary terms, though the literal 'can't raise money' is overstated given $67B raised. Nothing in it shows these constraints create a binding inability to fund AI's continuing needs, and nothing shows they don't. The data is US-only. The causal link is unsettled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: An unhedged 'will' with only 'at some point' as the horizon, so it is a scored forecast with no deadline. The chain from token-cost parity to lower value to fewer subscribers is kept.

contract.note: Context points to Anthropic and OpenAI. Requiring a cost-parity change, lost value and a fall in paid subscribers is a fair plain reading. A finite period without the event correctly does not refute the forecast.

evidence.note: Anthropic's May 2026 support page says usage bundles are optional extras and included usage is unchanged. It shows no parity change and gives no subscriber data.
OpenAI's September 2026 disclosure gives weekly active reach, not paid subscribers or any response to a cost-parity policy.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. The packet shows no documented cost-parity allowance change at either provider and no data on paid-subscriber declines. Not having happened yet is not failure under an open horizon.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Revision 2 keeps both 'for the most part' and 'every case I've found'. The proposition matches the statement.

contract.note: Context about per-million-token pricing suggests he means API-equivalent value. The contract defaults to provider expense but requires API-equivalent value to be reported separately, which is acceptable. The March 1–30 window is inferred. The examined cases are never listed, so the reading of 'token cost' decides the result.

evidence.note: An independent March 2026 measurement shows Claude reports usage as a percentage, not tokens. That supports masking for one provider only. The excerpt has no cost figures, and API-equivalent value is not provider expense.

reviews.rationale: Masking is supported for Claude's interface only, and one interface does not show what most subscriptions do. The packet has no matched usage and cost records for the speaker's examined cases, under either provider expense or API-equivalent value. The claim cannot be settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own 'pale horse' list in his newsletter.

semantics.note: This is a diagnostic claim: price rises or service cuts indicate a cash shortage, so it asserts a cause behind future changes rather than forecasting a definite event. The antecedent and both companies are kept.

contract.note: Testing each qualifying change against contemporaneous liquidity, with no added threshold, is fair. Treating it as a forecast rather than a causal diagnosis does not change what evidence is needed.

evidence.note: The April 4, 2026 removal of third-party harness use from subscription limits meets the antecedent but says nothing on cash. The company cited usage patterns and sustainability.
Anthropic's May 2026 post links higher limits to new compute. That suggests a capacity explanation but does not prove why April's restriction happened.
The S-1 shows $112.4B cash at June 30, 2026, which argues against a general shortage. It is measured at a different date after further financing, so it does not settle April. It is a company filing.

reviews.rationale: A qualifying service reduction happened in April 2026. No matched April liquidity records show whether Anthropic was or was not running low on cash. The June cash figure and the capacity explanation weigh against the claim but do not settle the April cause. No OpenAI episode is documented.
